editions.title: Anthropic's record IPO fails to steady markets as AI rout deepens
editions.notification: Anthropic's record IPO couldn't stop an AI rout: S&P 500 in correction and Asian markets heading for their worst week since 2020.
editions.intro:
Markets are the main story. Anthropic's $81bn Nasdaq debut at $83 a share was the largest IPO on record, but the shares have since slid and the wider AI trade has sold off hard. The S&P 500 fell 3.59% on Friday to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and more than 10% below its October record, which puts it in correction. The Dow has also entered correction, the Nasdaq has given up its 2026 gains, and Taiwan, Japan and South Korea have fallen sharply. Nvidia, still without a permanent chief after Jensen Huang's resignation and an affair scandal, has been among the heaviest fallers, and the SEC and California's attorney general are now probing the company.

The Gulf and Ukraine are the other pressure points. Iran fired missiles and drones at US sites in Kuwait and Bahrain after US strikes near Hormuz, the second military exchange since a memorandum of understanding was signed last week. Trump is reportedly weighing new strikes on Iran, and oil markets are watching closely. On the diplomatic side, Trump, Xi and Putin met at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, but produced only a broad four-point declaration and no breakthroughs on nuclear arms. Europeans fret about being sidelined. Meanwhile a Russian cruise missile crashed in Poland during a NATO exercise, and Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge again.

At home, Andy Burnham signed a reset deal with the EU covering food, carbon trading and a youth mobility scheme for up to 100,000 people a year. Farage and Badenoch attacked it, and the EU has tied parts of it to tuition fees for EU students. Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, and the Bank of England has raised rates to 4%.

editions.title: Anthropic's record IPO meets an Asian AI rout and Gulf strikes
editions.notification: Anthropic's $83 IPO was a record, yet AI stocks slid across Asia and Wall Street. Iran's strikes on Gulf bases widen.
editions.intro:
Anthropic's record stock market debut dominated the day, raising about $81bn at $83 a share and opening at $111.50 on Nasdaq. The euphoria did not spread. US indices fell more than 2% and the S&P 500 has now dropped six days running, while Asian markets are heading for their worst week since 2020, with Taiwan down 16%. Investors appear to be weighing a huge new supply of AI equity against stretched valuations, and Nvidia's shares have been hit since Jensen Huang's resignation.

The Gulf conflict also escalated. Iran fired missiles and drones at US sites in Kuwait and Bahrain after US strikes near the Strait of Hormuz, the second exchange since a memorandum of understanding was signed last week. Houthi missiles damaged parts of Riyadh, including the kingdom's tallest tower, and oil and shipping risks rose again.

Diplomacy at the APEC summit in Shenzhen produced a trilateral meeting of Trump, Xi and Putin, but little of substance. Nuclear arms control, Ukraine and AI were left open, and Putin ruled out a limited ceasefire after the Crimean Bridge was struck again. Nvidia's search for a new chief executive has reportedly reached Arm's Rene Haas, while the Bank of England, the IMF and the ECB all point to tighter money ahead.

editions.title: Trump, Xi and Putin set to meet as Ukraine hits Crimean Bridge
editions.notification: Trump, Xi and Putin are set for a first three-way nuclear meeting in Shenzhen, as Ukraine cuts Crimea's road link.
editions.intro:
Attention in Shenzhen is on the first in-person meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, due on Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit. The White House has confirmed the trilateral, which is expected to focus on nuclear arms control after New START expired in February, though China has not formally confirmed it and Moscow says the format is not yet agreed. A senior US official said no agreement is expected. Trump has left the summit early, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent representing the US at some sessions. Beijing has called the meeting groundbreaking, while critics describe it as a "New Yalta" moment.

The wider conflict is adding pressure. Iran has fired drones and missiles at US sites in Bahrain and Kuwait after American strikes, and a Hormuz tanker fire has put a US-Iran memorandum at risk. Ukraine has partly collapsed the Crimean Bridge, and a third attack reportedly hit it on the same week. Separately, Nvidia has posted record revenue under interim chief Colette Kress, but its board has ruled out Jensen Huang's return, and Washington has widened AI chip export curbs, with Congress now moving to tighten them further.

Markets are dealing with several strands at once. Anthropic has priced its IPO at $83 a share, making it the largest stock-market debut on record, with trading on the Nasdaq due on Thursday. Gold has fallen to its weakest level since September 2025 as markets price a possible US rate rise, and Deutsche Bank has fallen sharply after a leak of internal records. In the UK, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to sign an EU food and farming reset at a Friday summit, which he says shows Brexit "has not worked".

editions.title: Trump, Xi and Putin set for Shenzhen summit as Iran fight widens
editions.notification: Trump, Xi and Putin are set to meet in Shenzhen, as Iran strikes reach Kuwait and Bahrain and Nvidia's Huang fallout deepens.
editions.intro:
The biggest story is the first planned in-person meeting of Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, set for Thursday on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen. The White House has confirmed it, though China and the Kremlin have not fully done so, and no agreement is expected. Nuclear arms control is the main agenda item, following the expiry of New START in February. The meeting is being overshadowed by escalation in the Gulf. Iran has fired drones and missiles at US facilities in Bahrain and Kuwait after American strikes, and Qeshm Island was reportedly hit. Most projectiles were intercepted, but the attacks threaten the US-Iran memorandum that opened a 60-day negotiating window.

Alongside the summit, US export policy is tightening. Washington has required licences for advanced chip exports to five more countries and closed a loophole allowing remote access to Chinese computing power, while the Justice Department confirmed a criminal probe into Megaspeed. Nvidia's position is at the centre of this. It posted record revenue of $115.8bn, but its board has ruled out bringing back Jensen Huang, who resigned over an affair with a woman US officials suspect of Chinese intelligence links. Congress is moving on chip export bills, and Nvidia shares remain about 30% below their record high.

Elsewhere, Ukraine's strike on the Kerch bridge and the Crimean Bridge has cut a key supply route for Russia, timed ahead of the Shenzhen meeting. Oil prices are sensitive to the Gulf and Red Sea, where Houthis now control Bab al-Mandab. In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham is due to sign an EU reset deal in Brussels on Friday.

editions.title: Nvidia's Huang exit deepens; Iran strikes widen before Trump-Xi-Putin summit
editions.notification: Nvidia's leadership crisis deepens as US chip curbs tighten and Trump heads to a historic Shenzhen summit.
editions.intro:
Nvidia's leadership crisis remains the day's biggest story, and it is now spilling into policy and markets. Jensen Huang's resignation over an affair with a woman US officials suspect of working for Chinese intelligence has prompted fresh reporting on his wife's links to Chinese state-backed businesses, a New York Times account of his daughter Madison's influence, and talk of a return campaign backed by Elon Musk. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and the company reports its first results without Huang on 17 November. Meanwhile the US has widened AI chip export licensing to five more countries and closed a remote-access loophole, while Congress moves towards tighter rules, and Washington's own cabinet is openly divided over how hard to press Beijing.

The wider backdrop is a sharp tech sell-off. Intel plunged after a weak forecast, Alphabet had its worst day on record, and Nasdaq futures fell as investors demanded proof of returns on AI spending. Asian chip stocks slid again, and the ECB and Anthropic's large Nasdaq listing have added to fears of an AI repricing. Anthropic is set to list this week, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's remarks on AI scenarios come as markets price a likely December rate rise.

Geopolitics is equally heavy. US strikes on southern Iran have triggered attacks on US bases across the Gulf for a seventh night, and US intelligence reportedly puts Iran's missile stock at up to 2,500, undermining administration claims. Houthis now control the Bab al-Mandab Strait after Saudi-backed forces withdrew, pushing oil higher. Trump, Xi and Putin are due to meet at APEC in Shenzhen on Thursday, the first in-person trilateral, though no agreement is expected.

editions.title: Iran strikes spread as Nvidia's Huang fallout and Xi-Putin-Trump summit loom
editions.notification: US-Iran strikes enter a seventh night, Nvidia's leadership crisis deepens, and a first Xi-Putin-Trump summit is set.
editions.intro:
The conflict with Iran is the lead story again, now in its seventh consecutive night of strikes. Iranian missiles and drones have targeted US bases in Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait, and reports say at least five people died in a strike on a wedding in Kuhestak. Kuwait suspended operations at its international airport, and Iran's energy ministry asked citizens to cut power use after strikes on the grid. Separately, reports say the Trump administration warned Gulf allies that hostilities could resume as soon as Wednesday. Figures from both sides are unverified, and the White House has not confirmed any timing.

The second thread is Nvidia. Jensen Huang's resignation as chief executive, after reports of affairs including one with a Singapore-based executive US officials say was recruited by Chinese intelligence, has wiped roughly $600bn from the company's value in a week. Colette Kress is interim chief executive, and the first results without Huang are due on 17 November. Lawmakers are pressing for testimony, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is under scrutiny, and Huang reportedly discussed a return. Bessent has called for a "dramatic shakeup".

Diplomacy and markets are tied to both. A first in-person Xi-Trump-Putin meeting is set for Shenzhen during APEC, with nuclear arms on the agenda. Anthropic's IPO, priced at up to $1.4tn, is due to price on 18 November. Oil is elevated, with Brent near $94 to $96, and the Fed is signalling possible rate rises, which pushed the dollar to a 19-month high.

Finance.summary:

The S&P 500 fell 3.59% to 6,918.45 on Friday, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing run since February 2020, leaving it more than 10% below its October record. The Dow entered correction territory and the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the fall, with Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%, and the VIX topped 30 for the first time since March.

The sell-off has been fed by doubts about whether the AI spending boom can pay off, Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's chief executive, and a Democratic sweep in the midterms that raised fears of tighter AI rules. Anthropic's record IPO, which raised about $81bn, has not steadied things: its shares gave back much of Thursday's 17% gain. The slide has spread to Asia, where Taiwan's index fell 5.65% and Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each dropped about 5%.

Elsewhere, Bayer won final court approval for its $7.25bn Roundup settlement, the Bank of England's rate-setting is back in focus after UK inflation rose to 3.6%, and Iran's clash with US forces near Hormuz keeps oil risks elevated.

Both are leaning on domestic chips such as Huawei's, which still lag global leaders.

Anthropic's debut remains the defining event in the sector. Its shares rose on the first day, and its chief executive said AI carries "very real" but avoidable risks. The mood is mixed, though. Fashion.title: Burberry rebounds as Capri names new CEO
Fashion.notification: Burberry swings back to profit as Capri names a new chief executive and luxury looks for growth beyond China.
Fashion.summary:
The biggest story in fashion and luxury today is the Nvidia governance shock, though it sits at the edge of the sector, not inside it. Reports say chief executive Jensen Huang has resigned after claims of extramarital relationships, one with a suspected Chinese agent, and Nvidia shares fell more than 11%. Within luxury, the clearest good news came from Burberry, which swung back to a £54m first-half profit on 6% revenue growth, with wholesale up 17% and the Americas up 12%.

Leadership change is a theme across the sector. Capri has named Estée Lauder veteran Justin Boxford as chief executive from 4 January, ending John Idol's long run, while Tod's has parted ways with creative director Matteo Tamburini. Burberry's Daniel Lee profile and Zimmermann's expansion plans add to the picture of brands leaning on creative direction and new markets.

Demand is the underlying worry. Luxury groups are reportedly turning to the United States as the Chinese growth engine stalls, and Gulf shoppers are cutting back as war-linked inflation bites. Coach and Ralph Lauren are reportedly bucking China's slump, while On Holding posted record sales and margins, helped by tariff refunds.

Tech.title: Asia chip stocks rout deepens as AI fears grow
Tech.notification: Asian chip stocks slump as Anthropic's IPO turns into a sell-the-news event. Taiwan heads for its worst week since 1991.
Tech.summary:
Asian chip and AI stocks fell sharply after Anthropic's blockbuster listing turned into a sell-the-news event. Taiwan's Taiex dropped as much as 6.4% and is heading for its worst week since 1991, Japan's Nikkei hit its lowest since April, and SK Hynix and Samsung each fell more than 7%. Hong Kong's Hang Seng came close to a bear market. Investors are weighing worries about AI infrastructure spending, circular financing and new US curbs on China's access to advanced chips.

The squeeze is hitting China's tech giants too. New US rules stop Chinese firms from remotely using cutting-edge Nvidia chips in data centres abroad. Tencent says this will slow its model training in the short run, and Alibaba has warned that cloud growth could ease next year. Both are leaning on domestic chips such as Huawei's, which still lag global leaders.

Anthropic's debut remains the defining event in the sector. Its shares rose on the first day, and its chief executive said AI carries "very real" but avoidable risks. The mood is mixed, though. Gains for the newly listed company sit alongside a wider sell-off in AI names, with Nvidia reportedly down about 30% over the past month.

Finance.title: Wall Street's worst slide since February 2020 deepens as AI sell-off spreads
Finance.notification: The S&P 500 is in correction after seven losing sessions as the AI sell-off spreads to Asia.
Finance.summary:
US stocks have taken a heavy beating. The S&P 500 fell 3.59% to 6,918.45 on Friday, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing run since February 2020, leaving it more than 10% below its October record. The Dow entered correction territory and the Nasdaq erased all of its 2026 gains. Chipmakers led the fall, with Nvidia, Micron, Broadcom and AMD down roughly 12% to 14%, and the VIX topped 30 for the first time since March.

The sell-off has been fed by doubts about whether the AI spending boom can pay off, Jensen Huang's resignation as Nvidia's chief executive, and a Democratic sweep in the midterms that raised fears of tighter AI rules. Anthropic's record IPO, which raised about $81bn, has not steadied things: its shares gave back much of Thursday's 17% gain. The slide has spread to Asia, where Taiwan's index fell 5.65% and Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's Kospi each dropped about 5%.

Elsewhere, Bayer won final court approval for its $7.25bn Roundup settlement, the Bank of England's rate-setting is back in focus after UK inflation rose to 3.6%, and Iran's clash with US forces near Hormuz keeps oil risks elevated.

World.notification: Asian shares head for their worst week since 2020 as the AI sell-off deepens, despite Anthropic's record debut.
World.summary:
Markets are the main story of the day. Asian shares are heading for their worst week since March 2020 as an AI-driven sell-off deepens, with Taiwan down about 16% and Japan's Nikkei and South Korea's KOSPI also heading for steep weekly losses. Anthropic's record market debut, valuing it at up to $2.1 trillion, failed to lift the wider sector, and US indices fell over 2% overnight. The dollar has rallied on safe-haven demand, pushing gold towards its worst week in eight months.

Politically, the Trump, Xi and Putin trilateral in Shenzhen produced little of substance, with no breakthroughs on nuclear arms control or Ukraine. Europe is alarmed by reports of Trump urging a halt to funding for Ukraine, and a Russian cruise missile crashing in Poland has raised the temperature on NATO's eastern flank. In London, the FTSE 100 closed at a six-week low after the UK and EU agreed a reset package on youth mobility and food trade.

Fashion.title: Tod's refinancing and Armani stake talks reshape luxury
Fashion.notification: Tod's nears a €400m refinancing while L'Oréal reportedly eyes a stake in Armani
Fashion.summary:
Italian luxury is in the spotlight. Tod's is reportedly close to a €400 million refinancing led by Intesa Sanpaolo and BNP Paribas, with the Della Valle family ready to inject up to €60 million of equity if targets are missed. It follows a weak 2025, when revenue fell 7.7% and EBITDA dropped 16%, and comes after the group lost its creative director and its chief executive is leaving.

Armani is the other big story. Corriere della Sera reports that L'Oréal may take 10% of the house and EssilorLuxottica a further 5%, with LVMH reportedly out of the race. Heirs must sell around 15% by early March under Giorgio Armani's will. Neither side has confirmed a deal, so these remain reports.

Elsewhere, Schiaparelli's former chief executive Delphine Bellini has moved to Louis Vuitton, Dior signed Hyunjin as ambassador, and Ganni is closing its China flagship. Together they show brands rethinking ownership, talent and China.
